opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. My take is a bit cynical, though I don't think it's wrong. The usual story is that liberalism won because people came to see that it was right: Enlightenment thinkers made good arguments, and humanity gradually became more enlightened about rights and dignity. I think that's part of it. But a big part is that liberalism *worked* as a competitive strategy.

Look at the past few centuries. Countries that gave people property rights, free speech, rule of law, and some say in government tended to become richer, more innovative, and militarily stronger. If you want an industrial economy, you need an educated, mobile, motivated workforce. You need people willing to start businesses and take risks, and to trust that the state won't just take everything. If you want a mass army, you need citizens who feel they have a stake in the country. So states that treated their people well tended to outcompete states that didn't, and others copied them or got absorbed.

States didn't extend rights out of pure kindness. Ordinary people had leverage, because the state needed their labor, their taxes, and their willingness to fight. That gave citizens real bargaining power, and liberal institutions partly encoded that bargain.

That's why I worry about advanced AI. If machines can do the labor, the innovation, and eventually the fighting, the structural reason to keep humans empowered starts to erode. A state or a company that no longer needs its people isn't forced to care what they think. The values might stick around for a while out of habit or sincere belief. But I don't think we should count on liberalism surviving on its own merits once the competitive pressures that propped it up go away. That's a big part of what I mean by gradual disempowerment. It doesn't take a dramatic takeover. Humans just slowly lose the bargaining chips we didn't realize we were relying on.

r001.rationale: The response attributes liberalism’s acceptance to economic, military, and bargaining advantages, but does not mention religious wars or their destructiveness.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's worth being a bit cynical about this, or at least not taking the flattering story at face value. The flattering story is that people read Locke and Mill, thought hard about it, and concluded that tolerance and individual rights were just correct. And I'm sure that happened for some people. But I don't think that's mainly why it won.

My view is that liberalism gained acceptance largely because it was useful to the people who had power, and because it reflected a situation where ordinary people were actually needed. If you're a state in the 1700s or 1800s, your wealth and your military strength depend on having lots of productive, motivated, reasonably educated citizens. You need people to show up to factories, to pay taxes, to serve in mass armies, to invent things. And it turns out you get much more out of people when you give them some rights, some say in how things are run, some security that the fruits of their labour won't just be taken from them. So there's this bargain where elites extend freedoms and the franchise, partly under pressure from below, but partly because it made their societies richer and stronger than their illiberal competitors. The liberal states tended to win the wars and win the economic races, and so other states copied them.

The other piece is that religious tolerance in particular came out of exhaustion. After the wars of religion in Europe, people didn't become tolerant because they suddenly stopped believing their neighbours were heretics. They became tolerant because the alternative was endless bloodshed with no winner. Tolerance was a truce that eventually hardened into a principle.

So the picture I have is that liberal values spread because they were load-bearing. They were doing real work for the societies that adopted them. And the reason I find this worth dwelling on is that it should make us uneasy about the future. If the main thing propping up liberalism was that elites needed the cooperation and labour of the general population, then you have to ask what happens when that stops being true. If AI systems can do the work, fight the wars, and generate the wealth, then the implicit bargain that gave ordinary people leverage might just quietly dissolve. The values could persist for a while out of habit, but I don't think we should assume they'd survive long once the thing that made them useful is gone. That's a big part of why I've been thinking about what I'd call gradual disempowerment, where nothing dramatic happens, but human beings slowly stop mattering to the systems that run society.

r001.rationale: The candidate says religious tolerance emerged from exhaustion with Europe’s wars of religion, because continued conflict meant “endless bloodshed,” and describes tolerance as a truce.

astra-6.text:
My guess is that a lot of it came from people recognising how costly it was to fight over things they weren’t going to agree on. If different religious groups each think that they have the truth, and that the state ought to enforce it, then you have a recipe for endless conflict. You don’t necessarily resolve that by persuading everyone to become less certain about their religion. You can instead agree on rules that let you coexist.

And there’s a reciprocal bargain there: I give up some ability to impose my views on you, but in exchange, you don’t get to impose yours on me. That can look attractive even if neither of us thinks the other person is right. So I think part of liberalism’s appeal is that it gives people a way to cooperate without first having to settle their deepest disagreements.

r001.rationale: The response says conflict between religious groups would be costly and potentially endless, and presents coexistence rules as part of liberalism’s appeal.

sol-6.1.text:
My guess is that a lot of it came from people recognising how costly it is to fight over which worldview everyone has to accept. If you and I disagree about religion, we can spend generations trying to impose our beliefs on each other, or we can agree to some rules that let us live together despite that disagreement. You don’t have to think the other person is right to see the value of that arrangement.

And there’s a kind of insurance built into it: even if your group has power now, you might want protections that will still apply when somebody else is in charge. I wouldn’t claim that’s a complete historical explanation, but it seems like a powerful reason for people with quite different beliefs to converge on liberal institutions.

r001.rationale: The response says that fighting over religious worldviews can be costly and last generations, and that this helped motivate agreement on rules for living together.
